title: Praying with the saints
hookLine: Catholics and Orthodox ask the saints to pray for them; Protestant churches pray to God alone

cards: Pray for me. People say it in hospital corridors, text it before a job interview, whisper it at a graveside. Paul asks the Romans to strive together with him in their prayers.
James tells his readers, plainly, to pray one for another. On that much, the text is clear. The question comes when the person you'd ask has died.
Can you ask a saint in heaven to pray for you, the way you'd ask a friend down the hall? The churches answer differently.

teach.b: Intercession means praying on someone else's behalf, standing in for them before God. Paul urges it in his first letter to Timothy: "supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men."
Catholics and Orthodox Christians ask the saints to pray for them. Their reasoning: those who died in Christ are alive in God, not gone.
So asking Mary or Saint Peter to pray for you is like asking a friend who is now very near to God. They are careful to say this is not worship; worship belongs to God alone.
They point to Revelation, where elders before the Lamb hold "golden vials full of odours, which are the prayers of saints." Protestant churches, following the Reformers, direct prayer to God alone.
They point to the same letter to Timothy, a few lines later: "there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Protestants still ask one another to pray, gladly.
They keep those requests among the living, and bring everything else straight to God through Christ. Then there's a verse both sides read closely, in Hebrews.

teach.h: SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.
teach.b: After a long roll call of faithful people, Abraham and Sarah, Moses and Rahab, it says: "we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses."
Catholics and Orthodox hear the saints praying alongside the living. Protestants hear a crowd of examples, lives that still testify.
Either way, the next words, "let us run with patience," put the runner in a full stadium, not an empty one.

how: Catholics and Orthodox Christians ask saints, especially Mary, to pray for them, and keep saints' days through the year; Protestant Christians pray to God through Christ and ask fellow believers to pray for them.

games.q: intercession in the text — tap the pairs.
p: so great a cloud of witnesses

s: Catholics and Orthodox call asking the saints worship
they say worship belongs to God alone; asking a saint is like asking a friend to pray.
Protestants ask one another to pray
gladly. they direct prayer to God alone, and keep their requests among the living.
the cloud of witnesses comes after a roll call of faithful people
Abraham and Sarah, Moses and Rahab; then Hebrews 12:1 calls them a cloud of witnesses.

games.q: a friend is going into surgery tomorrow. she asks, "will you pray for me?" what does the letter of James say?
games.why: "pray one for another, that ye may be healed." the churches in today's teach all pray for the living; they differ on asking the saints.

practice: Bring to mind one person of faith whose life still speaks to you: Francis, or Peter, or Mary herself, or a grandmother who prayed every morning, a teacher who showed you patience.
Recall one thing they did or said that you'd like to carry into your week, and hold it for a while. If you pray, thank God for that life; if you don't, say their name quietly, and keep the one thing.

wordCard.voice: Intercession. Praying on behalf of someone else. Every church here does it for the living; they differ on asking the saints to join in.

orig.note: Greek: a petition on someone's behalf; the word behind "intercessions" in 1 Timothy 2:1.

carryVoice: Your line: the cloud of witnesses. Pray one for another, as James puts it. Same time tomorrow.
